stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Groundwater recharge in desert basins is hard to measure, because most rainfall evaporates before it can soak into the ground. To get around this problem, Chilean hydrologist ______ buried temperature sensors beneath dry streambeds, reasoning that a sudden cooling of the sediment would mark the moment floodwater began to seep downward. Her readings showed that a few brief flash floods each year supply most of the basin's recharge.
explanation: There is no article before 'Chilean hydrologist,' so the title and the name work together as one label for the subject. The name tells you which hydrologist is meant, so nothing should separate it from the title. The subject 'Chilean hydrologist Paula Errázuriz' then leads straight into its verb, 'buried,' with no punctuation in between.

B.why: You treated the name as an extra appositive and set it off with a pair of commas. Without 'the' or 'a' before the title, the name is essential, so it can't be fenced off from the title.

C.why: You put a single comma after the name. That comma separates the subject, 'Chilean hydrologist Paula Errázuriz,' from its verb, 'buried,' and a lone comma can't go there.

D.why: You used a colon, but a colon needs a complete sentence before it. 'To get around this problem, Chilean hydrologist' is a fragment, so the colon interrupts the subject.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Concrete cracks as it ages, and water seeping through those cracks corrodes the steel reinforcement inside. Materials scientist ______ developed a mortar mixed with dormant bacterial spores and calcium lactate to slow this damage. When water enters a fresh crack, the spores wake up and produce limestone, sealing gaps up to nearly a millimeter wide without any human repair.
explanation: 'Materials scientist' has no article in front of it, so the title and the name form a single noun phrase naming the subject. Leave out all punctuation: 'Materials scientist Liesbeth Vandermeer developed...' keeps the subject and the verb together.

A.why: You used a pair of dashes as though the name were an interruption you could remove. Without an article, the name identifies which scientist is meant, so it is part of the subject and can't be fenced off.

C.why: You put an appositive comma between the title and the name. With no 'a' or 'the' before the title, the two belong together and nothing should separate them.

D.why: You put a comma after the name. That splits the subject, 'Materials scientist Liesbeth Vandermeer,' from its verb, 'developed.'

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Many cities widen roads to ease traffic, only to find that the new lanes fill with cars within a few years. Danish urban planner ______ argues that the reverse also holds: when streets are narrowed or closed to cars, much of the traffic does not move elsewhere but disappears, as residents switch to walking, cycling, or fewer trips.
explanation: Check the front of the title. There is no 'a' or 'the' before 'Danish urban planner,' so the title and the name act together as one label. No punctuation belongs between them, and none belongs between the name and the verb 'argues.'

A.why: You applied the appositive rule ('my friend, Ana, said') and set the name off with commas. That rule needs an article before the title. Here the name is essential and must stay attached.

B.why: You put a single comma after the name, which wedges punctuation between the subject and its verb, 'argues.'

D.why: You put a comma between the title and the name. Without an article, they form one noun phrase, so a comma there breaks up the subject.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Coaches have long assumed that athletes who sleep less recover more slowly, but few studies had measured the effect during an actual competitive season. Exercise physiologist ______ fitted thirty collegiate rowers with wrist monitors for an entire spring season. Rowers who averaged under seven hours of sleep showed slower drops in heart rate after hard sessions than teammates who slept longer.
explanation: No article comes before 'Exercise physiologist,' so the title and the name are one unit that names the subject. The subject runs directly into its verb, 'fitted,' with no punctuation anywhere in the phrase.

A.why: You put a comma after the name. That separates the subject, 'Exercise physiologist Adaeze Nwosu,' from its verb, 'fitted.'

B.why: You treated the name as a removable appositive and surrounded it with commas. Without 'the' or 'a' before the title, the name is essential and takes no commas.

C.why: You used a colon, but 'Exercise physiologist' is not a complete sentence, so it can't come before a colon.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Farmers in dry regions often leave fields bare between harvests, but exposed soil loses moisture quickly to wind and sun. Soil scientist ______ tested whether a low-growing clover planted after the wheat harvest would hold more water in the ground. Over three years, plots with clover kept noticeably more moisture in their top layer of soil than bare plots did.
explanation: 'Soil scientist' has no article before it, so the title and the name form a single noun phrase that names the subject. Don't put any punctuation between the title and the name, or between the name and the verb 'tested.'

A.why: You set off the name with a pair of commas as if it were extra information. With no article before the title, the name is essential and must stay attached to it.

B.why: You put a single comma after the name, which splits the subject from its verb, 'tested.'

D.why: You put a dash between the title and the name. A single dash works like a colon and needs a complete sentence before it. 'Soil scientist' is only part of the subject.
